claims.text: Adding approximately 1 wt% nanostructured Y2O3 particles to a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3 addition can preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
The Y2O3 addition is compatible with engineering practicality for plasma-facing applications.
Powder metallurgy or mechanical alloying followed by consolidation can produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles in the alloy matrix.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced interstitials.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as efficient sinks for radiation-induced vacancies.
Capture of irradiation-induced point defects by the oxide particles reduces void formation.
Capture of irradiation-induced point defects by the oxide particles reduces defect-cluster formation.
Y2O3 particles act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Dislocation pinning by Y2O3 particles maintains the alloy's strength during irradiation.
Dislocation pinning by Y2O3 particles maintains the alloy's ductility during irradiation.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will have approximately 20–30% lower void swelling or radiation-induced defect density.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will retain similar yield strength after irradiation.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the oxide-dispersed alloy will retain similar ductility after irradiation.
The predicted benefit depends on the oxide dispersion remaining stable and uniformly distributed during irradiation.
Significant oxide agglomeration may prevent the predicted radiation-tolerance benefit.
Substantial deviation from the target Y2O3 loading may prevent the predicted benefit.
